newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Lubricants lift Burmah's profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lubricants lift Burmah's profits.

text.p: The British lubricants and chemicals firm Burmah Castrol reported a 13 percent profit rise on Monday as its Asian lubricants operations continued to power ahead.
Net attributable income climbed to 67.7 million pounds ($105.4 million) from 59.9 million as Castrol lubricant volumes climbed 10 percent in Asia -- double the rate of market growth.
The profit figure excludes a 23.2 million pound gain stemming from the sale of fuels operations in Sweden, Turkey and Chile earlier this year.
Chief executive Jonathan Fry told Reuters that Asia would remain the main drive behind Burmah's results, thanks to the popularity of the Castrol brand name and the firm's experience in the region.

"It is a considerably successful story. We've got a lot of momentum there," Fry said. "It's really our understanding of the markets. We were in a number of them very early and our brand is very popular," he added.
Burmah expanded its Asian operations in June, when it set up a joint venture to target the fast growing Chinese lubricants market.
The joint venture with Shenzen Nanyou ((Holdings) Ltd currently employs 130 people, but Fry said this number will almost have doubled by the end of next year.

With the Brazilian lubricants operations led by a new management team and on track to become profitable again next year, Burmah only needs a pick-up in the German economy to power full steam ahead, Fry said.
Speaking of the overall group results, which met analysts' expectations, Fry said: "Obviously they would have been better, but for the situation in continental Europe, led by Germany."
"But taking that drag effect into account we are satisfied with the results," he added.
Fry, however, was optimistic that the German economy was getting stronger, which would have a positive impact on Burmah's lubricants as well as its chemical results.
Three of the four chemical units saw their results rise in the first half, but metallurgical chemicals was hit by a slowdown in steel production and de-stocking in the motor trade.
The overall chemicals operations saw a seven percent increase in operating profit, pushed higher by strong growth at the screen printing ink division in particular.

Chemicals and lubricants are Burmah's core businesses. For some time Burmah has been negotiating to divest its Pakistani gas investments. Fry said it was a "long-running saga", complicated by local politics.
He added that Burmah may also decide in due course to get out of its Asian LNG tranportation business where it works with Japanse partner Mitsui O.S.K. Lines.
"It would be a complicated business to divest, but it is obvious that it is not part of our core business," Fry said.
But before making any decisions here, Burmah wants to secure transport contracts for all of its vessels, Fry said.
Six out of eight ships already have long-term contracts.

"At the moment we are still in the process of tying up our last two ships. That is our priority and then (we will) consider our strategic position," he said. "We would have to talk to our partners about what their intentions are."
Burmah shares rose 15 pence to 1065 in late morning trade.
"Overall it was a pleasing performance. The prospective ratings are below market average and it's one of the cheapest stocks in the sector," said analyst Irene Himona at SG Strauss Turnbull.
